numerical_failure.affected_api: pandas.read_csv (C parser TextReader._column_has_float in pandas/_libs/parsers.pyx, module pandas._libs.parsers)
numerical_failure.observed_behavior: Large floating-point numbers in a read_csv column are read as strings instead of floats, because integer parsing is attempted first; large integers without a decimal separator or exponent are also still read as strings.
numerical_failure.expected_behavior: Large floating-point numbers should be read into float dtype. A column containing a decimal separator or exponent sign (e/E) should be detected as float and parsed as float, e.g. 18446744073709551616.0 should read as float(1 << 64) and 36893488147419103232.3 as float(1 << 65).
trigger_conditions: CSV column contains large floating-point numbers that overflow integer parsing
column value contains a decimal separator or exponent sign (e/E) indicating a float
float_precision parameter across all parser precisions (all_parsers_all_precisions)
oracle_clues: Test for exponent and no-decimal-separator cases added in the PR

numerical_characteristics.precision: float_precision parameter over all parser precisions (all_parsers_all_precisions); large values such as 18446744073709551616.0 lose precision when read as float
numerical_characteristics.magnitude: values beyond 2^64 (e.g. 18446744073709551616.0 = float(1 << 64), 36893488147419103232.3 = float(1 << 65)); also exponent-form values such as 3.2e80 and 3.2e-80
category_specific_evidence: Test test_small_int_followed_by_float parametrizes values like 32.0, 3.2e1, 3.2e80, 3.2e-80 and large values 18446744073709551616.0 and 36893488147419103232.3, comparing via tm.assert_frame_equal against float(1 << 64) and float(1 << 65), marked 'loses precision'.
Fix (GH#51295) skips integer parsing for a column when a potential float is detected by a decimal separator or exponent sign (e/E), so large floats are read as float instead of strings.
Commit notes state large floats may experience precision loss due to floating-point representation; a comment makes the precision loss explicit.
Discussion states floats beyond 2^64 suffer precision loss and that performance overhead of the added check is a concern (overhead reduced from 2.83 to 2.47 in verification).
Large integers are still read as strings and are not addressed by this change (tested in test_ints.py).
reproduction_risks: Expected values in the test are the nearest float (float(1 << 64)), so exact-decimal comparison will not match; comparison must allow the floating-point rounding of the input.
Large integer inputs without decimal separator or exponent remain strings, so reproduction must not expect float conversion for them.
Parsing across all precisions (all_parsers_all_precisions) may behave differently per float_precision setting.
